name: Dresden Codex
info: The Dresden Codex is a Maya screenfold book of bark paper from the Yucatán Peninsula, probably from the Chichen Itza region, dated to the 11th or 12th century, holding astronomical tables, ritual schedules and medicine, and now kept in Dresden.

facts.made: Eight different scribes, who painted with thin brushes and vegetable dyes; Maya of the Yucatán Peninsula, probably the Chichen Itza region according to J. Eric S. Thompson, copying an original text some three or four hundred years older
facts.form: A screenfold book of 78 pages of amate, about 20 centimetres high, 3.7 metres long when unfolded, written in Maya hieroglyphs, with decorative board covers
facts.where: The Saxon State and University Library Dresden (SLUB Dresden), Germany
facts.known: Detailed Venus tables; lunar tables with intervals correlating with eclipses; a 260-day ritual calendar; the Maya new-year ceremony; the rain god Chaac, shown 134 times; its role in the decipherment of Maya hieroglyphs; water damage in 1945

t: The codex is a Maya screenfold book from the Yucatán Peninsula, probably from the area of Chichen Itza, and scholars place its making between the 11th and 14th centuries.
Its pages hold accurate astronomical tables, notably for Venus and the Moon, together with ritual schedules, religious references, and information on seasons, illness and medicine.
It survived the Spanish Inquisition, reached Dresden in 1739 and was damaged in the bombing of Dresden in 1945; it later played a key role in deciphering Maya hieroglyphs.
dyk: The Dresden Codex is one of four hieroglyphic Maya codices that survived the Spanish Inquisition in the New World. After it spent February 1945 in a flooded basement during the bombing of Dresden, the sheets 6/40, 7/39 and 8/38 were put back in reverse order when they were returned to their glass cabinet.
ev: The codex is made, probably as a copy of an original text some three or four hundred years older
Johann Christian Götze buys the codex from a private owner in Vienna
Alexander von Humboldt publishes pages 47, 48 and 50 to 52, the first reproduction of any of its pages
Lord Kingsborough publishes the first copy of the codex in his Antiquities of Mexico
Ernst Wilhelm Förstemann publishes the first complete facsimile and deciphers its calendar section
Paul Schellhas assigns letters to the gods named by its glyphs
The codex is kept in a flooded basement during the bombing of Dresden and suffers serious water damage
Yuri Knorozov applies a phonetic approach based on the De Landa alphabet to decode the codex

sections.origins:
The Dresden Codex is a Maya book from the Yucatán Peninsula in southeastern Mexico. The historian J. Eric S. Thompson describes it as writings of the indigenous people of the peninsula, and the Maya historians Peter J. Schmidt, Mercedes de la Garza and Enrique Nalda confirm this. Thompson narrows its probable origin to the area of Chichen Itza, because certain picture symbols in the codex are found only on monuments there, and he argues that its astronomical tables support the same place. He adds that the people of the Yucatán Peninsula were known to have made such studies around 1200 CE, and he notes similar ceramic designs in the Chichen Itza area that are known to have ceased in the early thirteenth century.

Its date is given in several ways. It is dated to the 11th or 12th century. The British historian Clive Ruggles, drawing on the analyses of several scholars, suggests that it is a copy, originally written between the twelfth and fourteenth centuries. Thompson narrows the date closer to 1200 to 1250, and the Maya archaeologist Linton Satterthwaite puts the date when it was made at no later than 1345. The codex also refers to an original text of some three or four hundred years earlier, describing local history and astronomical tables.
sections.content:
The codex contains 78 pages, and most have writing on both sides. Each page is generally divided into three horizontal sections, which students of the codex have arbitrarily labelled a, b and c; some pages have only two, while one has four and another five. Sections with a theme of their own are generally separated by a red vertical line and divided into two to four columns. The book holds information relating to astronomical and astrological tables, religious references, the seasons of the earth, and illness and medicine, as well as conjunctions of planets and moons.

Its astronomy is recognised by students of the codex for the detailed Venus tables and lunar tables. The lunar series has intervals correlating with eclipses, and the Venus tables correlate with the movements of the planet. Ruggles shows that in the codex the Maya related their 260-day calendar to celestial bodies, especially Venus and Mars. The codex also contains astrological tables and ritual schedules. Its religious references show, in a cycle of the 260-day ritual calendar, the important Maya royal events, and it includes information on the Maya new-year ceremony tradition. The rain god Chaac is represented 134 times.
sections.making:
Like all other pre-Hispanic books from Mesoamerica, the Dresden Codex takes the form of a screenfold. Its pages are made of amate, a paper from the pounded inner bark of a wild species of fig, Ficus cotinifolia, called hu'un in Maya, a word that became semantically equivalent to book. They are 20 centimetres high and can be folded accordion-style; unfolded, the codex is 3.7 metres long. The Maya codices all have pages of about the same size, about 20 centimetres high and 10 centimetres wide, and the Dresden Codex has decorative board covers on the front and back.

The pictures and glyphs were painted by skilled craftsmen using thin brushes and vegetable dyes. Black and red were the main colours on many pages, and some pages have detailed backgrounds in shades of yellow, green and the Maya blue. The pages have a border of red paint, although many have lost it to age. The codex was written by eight different scribes, who each had their own writing style, glyph designs and subject matter. It is written in Maya hieroglyphs and is thought to copy an earlier text.
sections.reception:
Reproductions of the codex began in the early nineteenth century. Alexander von Humboldt published pages 47, 48 and 50 to 52 in his 1810 atlas Vues des Cordillères et Monuments des Peuples Indigènes de l'Amérique, the first reproduction of any of its pages. In 1828 Constantine Samuel Rafinesque identified the book as Maya from its glyphs, which looked like those found at Palenque. The Italian artist Agostino Aglio began in 1826 to transcribe and illustrate the codex completely for Lord Kingsborough, who published it in the nine volumes of his Antiquities of Mexico in 1831 to 1848.

Later study centred on its numbers and gods. Ernst Wilhelm Förstemann, the Dresden librarian, published the first complete facsimile in 1880, deciphered the calendar section and its Maya numerals, and determined that the numbers, with deities and day names, related to the Maya calendar and the Long Count. The historian Cyrus Thomas connected the codex with the cycle of the Maya calendar and the 365 days of the year. In 1897 and 1904 Paul Schellhas assigned letters to the gods of particular glyphs, since they had several possible names: God D could be Hunab Ku Itzam Na among other names, and God A could be Cizin, a god of death.
sections.survival:
The Dresden Codex is one of four hieroglyphic Maya codices that survived the Spanish Inquisition in the New World. Johann Christian Götze, a German theologian and director of the Royal Library at Dresden, bought it from a private owner in Vienna in 1739 while travelling to Italy. Thompson speculates that Hernán Cortés sent it as tribute to Charles V, since examples of local writings and other Maya items were sent in 1519 to the ruler, who was then living in Vienna. It was catalogued into the Royal Library of Dresden in 1744 and remained relatively obscure until the early twentieth century.

By the time of the Kingsborough copies it had some damage from handling, sunlight and moisture. In February 1945, during the bombing of Dresden, it was kept in a flooded basement and received direct water damage that was significantly destructive. The German historian G. Zimmerman later noted that the damage was extreme on pages 2, 4, 24, 28, 34, 38, 71 and 72, and some details of the glyph images have been lost. The harm shows when the codex is compared with the Kingsborough copies and the Förstemann facsimiles of 1880 and 1892. Sheets 6/40, 7/39 and 8/38 were reversed by an error when they were returned to their protective glass cabinet after drying.
sections.legacy:
The codex has played a key role in deciphering Maya hieroglyphs. In the 1950s Yuri Knorozov used a phonetic approach based on the De Landa alphabet to decode it, and in the 1980s other scholars did further deciphering on the same concept. Schellhas's letters for the gods were meant as a noncommittal system and were adopted by later researchers of the Maya codices. Together with the Madrid and Paris codices, named after the cities where they were rediscovered, and the Maya Codex of Mexico, it is one of the four surviving hieroglyphic Maya books.

The page numbers in use today were assigned by Aglio in 1825 to 1826, when he divided the codex into two parts and labelled them Codex A and Codex B. In 1836 the librarian K. C. Falkenstein adjusted the position of pages for what he called esthetical reasons, producing the two parts of similar length, and Förstemann corrected Aglio's assignment of the sheets 1/45 and 2/44. Historians such as Helmut Deckert and Ferdinand Anders understand that a reading should run through the complete front side, pages 1 to 24 and 46 to 74, and then the back side, pages 25 to 45. The codex is held by the Saxon State and University Library Dresden.

summary: The Dresden Codex is a Maya screenfold book of bark paper, probably made around Chichen Itza and dated between the 11th and 14th centuries. It holds Venus and lunar tables and ritual schedules, reached Dresden in 1739, was damaged in 1945, and helped in deciphering Maya writing.

Helmut Deckert, Die Dresdner Maya-Handschrift (Akademische Druck-u. Verlagsanstalt, 1989)
John Eric Sidney Thompson, A Commentary on the Dresden Codex: A Maya Hieroglyphic Book (American Philosophical Society, 1972)
notes: Dating: the article says 11th or 12th century (and a source citing it as the earliest surviving book of the Americas), Thompson 1200-1250, Ruggles a copy written between the 12th and 14th centuries, Satterthwaite no later than 1345. start is 1200 with circa true.

The article calls the Dresden Codex 'one of the oldest surviving book written in the Americas' and also calls the Maya Codex of Mexico 'the oldest and only codex still located in the Americas'; the ranking claim is left out.
Size: 3.7 m unfolded in the lead, 3.56 m in the facsimile note; 78 pages, 74 with inscriptions in the facsimile note. The text uses 3.7 m and 78 pages.
Left out: the sentence linking Cyrus Thomas to the '260 year cycle (Ahau Katun)', which is garbled; only his link to the calendar cycle and 365 days is kept, loosely.
Aglio's transcription is dated 1826 in one place and 1825-26 in another; both are used as the article gives them.
Article's 'Spanish Inquisition in the New World' phrase kept as given. The 1892 Förstemann facsimile is named only in the damage comparison.
